rows.verified: Employers must control welding-fume health risks for specialist and occasional welders, regardless of how small the amount of welding is.
All welding fume can cause lung cancer and can also cause occupational asthma and other health conditions.
Welding fume is controlled under the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations.
Controls should be considered in the order: avoid or reduce exposure, use local exhaust ventilation, then use suitable respiratory protective equipment.
Indoor welding should use local exhaust ventilation to capture fume at source where welding cannot be avoided.
Suitable respiratory protective equipment is required where local exhaust ventilation does not adequately control exposure or is not reasonably practicable.
For outdoor welding, local exhaust ventilation is ineffective, so suitable respiratory protective equipment should be used.
Respiratory health surveillance should be provided where welding exposure creates a reasonable likelihood of occupational asthma, such as exposure to asthmagens in stainless-steel fume.
Welding-fume controls depend on process, metal, coating, duration, location, enclosure, LEV capture, RPE fit and nearby-worker exposure.
Welding evidence is process-, material-, task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level cancer or asthma probability.
Wood dust can cause occupational asthma and dermatitis, and hardwood dust can cause a rare form of nasal cancer.
Wood-dust exposure must be prevented or adequately controlled under COSHH.
High-risk woods should be substituted where reasonably practicable.
Fixed local exhaust ventilation should control wood dust at source during machining.
Vacuum equipment used for cleaning wood dust should meet at least dust class M.
Respiratory protective equipment with a minimum assigned protection factor of 20, such as FFP3, is required for many machining and short dusty tasks.
Dry sweeping should be replaced with suitable vacuum cleaning to avoid redistributing wood dust.
COSHH assessments should include maintenance and cleaning tasks and involve workers who perform the actual work.
Wood-dust controls depend on wood species, composite material, machining process, dust generation, LEV performance, cleaning method and RPE use.
Wood-dust evidence is material-, process- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory or cancer probability.
